questions.tested_concept: High-dose biotin (vitamin B7) interference with streptavidin-biotin thyroid assays
questions.stem: A clinically euthyroid 35-year-old woman taking an over-the-counter high-dose hair-and-nail supplement has routine labs showing markedly suppressed TSH and markedly elevated free T₄, mimicking Graves disease. Her heart rate, weight, and thyroid exam are completely normal. Which supplement and mechanism best explain these discordant labs?
options: High-dose biotin interfering with streptavidin-biotin assays (false-low TSH, false-high free T₄)
Dietary seaweed iodine triggering the Wolff-Chaikoff effect (false-high TSH, false-low free T₄)
Over-the-counter calcium carbonate blocking levothyroxine absorption in the jejunum
St. John's wort inducing hepatic CYP3A4 clearance of endogenous pituitary TSH
questions.explanation: Step 1. A clinically euthyroid patient with severe apparent biochemical hyperthyroidism (low TSH + high free T₄) should immediately prompt a medication/supplement history for assay interference. Step 2. High-dose biotin (vitamin B₇) competes with biotinylated reagents in streptavidin-biotin immunoassays, causing false-low results on sandwich assays (like TSH) and false-high results on competitive assays (like free T₄/T₃).
choice_rationales: Excess biotin disrupts streptavidin-biotin lab platforms, producing a classic 'pseudo-Graves' pattern (false-low TSH, false-high free T₄) that resolves after holding biotin for 48–72 hours.
Wolff-Chaikoff from excess iodine causes true hypothyroidism (high TSH, low T₄), not a false-low TSH / false-high T₄ pattern.
Calcium carbonate impairs oral levothyroxine gut absorption in treated hypothyroid patients, raising TSH rather than mimicking Graves disease.
St. John's wort induces hepatic cytochrome P450 enzymes for steroid/drug metabolism rather than falsely altering TSH/free T₄ immunoassays.

questions.tested_concept: Amiodarone and lithium mechanisms of thyroid and renal endocrine disruption
questions.stem: A 64-year-old man started on amiodarone for atrial fibrillation develops thyroid dysfunction, while a 41-year-old woman on chronic lithium develops goiter and hypothyroidism. Which mechanistic pairing accurately describes how lithium and amiodarone disrupt thyroid physiology?
options: Lithium directly stimulates TSH receptors causing Graves disease; amiodarone selectively destroys parathyroid chief cells
Lithium inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis/release; amiodarone causes iodine excess and blocks 5'-deiodinase
Lithium blocks hepatic TBG synthesis causing low total T₄; amiodarone triggers biotin-like immunoassay interference
Lithium stimulates renal aquaporin-2 insertion causing SIADH; amiodarone accelerates peripheral T₄-to-T₃ conversion
questions.explanation: Step 1. Lithium concentrates in the thyroid gland and directly inhibits iodine uptake, thyroglobulin processing, and thyroid hormone release (causing hypothyroidism/goiter, alongside nephrogenic DI in the kidney). Step 2. Amiodarone is ~37% iodine by weight and inhibits 5'-deiodinase; it can cause hypothyroidism (Wolff-Chaikoff) or hyperthyroidism via Type 1 (Jod-Basedow iodine excess) or Type 2 (direct destructive thyroiditis).
choice_rationales: Lithium causes hypothyroidism (not Graves) and nephrogenic DI, and amiodarone targets the thyroid rather than parathyroid chief cells.

Lithium directly inhibits thyroid hormone synthesis/release, whereas iodine-rich amiodarone disrupts thyroid function via Wolff-Chaikoff, Jod-Basedow, destructive thyroiditis, and 5'-deiodinase inhibition.
Neither drug acts primarily through TBG depletion or streptavidin-biotin assay interference.
Lithium causes nephrogenic DI (AQP2 resistance, not SIADH), and amiodarone inhibits (not accelerates) peripheral T₄-to-T₃ conversion.

questions.tested_concept: Exogenous glucocorticoid (including inhaled & megestrol) HPA axis suppression
questions.stem: A 58-year-old man with severe COPD using high-dose inhaled fluticasone plus oral megestrol acetate for appetite stimulation develops fatigue, hypotension, and hyponatremia after abruptly stopping both agents. Morning cortisol and ACTH are both markedly low. What mechanism explains this presentation?
options: Megestrol acetate blocked peripheral glucocorticoid receptors, triggering compensatory ACTH elevation and hyperpigmentation
Inhaled corticosteroids directly destroyed the adrenal zona glomerulosa, causing primary Addison disease with high ACTH
Exogenous glucocorticoid activity suppressed HPA negative feedback, causing secondary adrenal insufficiency
Abrupt cessation triggered acute pituitary apoplexy with cavernous sinus ophthalmoplegia
questions.explanation: Step 1. Systemic absorption of high-dose inhaled glucocorticoids—as well as progestins with intrinsic glucocorticoid activity like megestrol acetate—exerts chronic negative feedback on hypothalamic CRH and pituitary ACTH. Step 2. Prolonged ACTH suppression causes adrenal fasciculata atrophy, so abrupt withdrawal precipitates iatrogenic secondary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol + low ACTH), requiring gradual tapering.
choice_rationales: Megestrol acts as a glucocorticoid agonist (suppressing ACTH), not an antagonist raising ACTH.
Primary Addison disease presents with elevated ACTH and aldosterone loss (hyperkalemia), whereas exogenous steroid suppression produces low ACTH.
Both high-dose inhaled corticosteroids and megestrol acetate suppress CRH/ACTH via negative feedback, so sudden cessation unmasks secondary adrenal insufficiency (low cortisol, low ACTH).
Pituitary apoplexy causes sudden thunderclap headache and diplopia from sellar hemorrhage, not quiet post-withdrawal HPA suppression.

questions.tested_concept: Estrogen-induced TBG elevation vs immune checkpoint inhibitor endocrinopathies
questions.stem:
Evaluate the following two statements regarding drug effects on endocrine testing and glands:

Statement 1: Oral estrogen-containing contraceptives increase hepatic thyroxine-binding globulin (TBG), raising total serum T₄ while free T₄ and TSH remain normal in a euthyroid patient.
Statement 2: Immune checkpoint inhibitors (such as CTLA-4 and PD-1 blockers) can trigger autoimmune endocrinopathies including hypophysitis, destructive thyroiditis, and autoimmune diabetes.
options: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; Statement 2 is true
questions.explanation: Step 1. Oral estrogens stimulate hepatic synthesis of binding globulins (TBG, CBG, SHBG), increasing total bound hormone levels without altering biologically active free T₄ or TSH in a patient with an intact thyroid axis. Step 2. Immune checkpoint inhibitors unleash T-cell autoimmunity against endocrine organs, classically causing lymphocytic hypophysitis (especially CTLA-4), thyroiditis, and immune-mediated Type 1 diabetes.
choice_rationales: Both statements accurately describe estrogen-driven TBG elevation (high total T₄, normal free T₄/TSH) and immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced autoimmune endocrinopathies.
Neither statement is false; both are key clinical traps emphasized in EX.10.
Statement 2 is also true because checkpoint inhibitors frequently cause autoimmune thyroiditis, hypophysitis, and adrenalitis/diabetes.
Statement 1 is also true because measuring free T₄ and TSH avoids mistaking estrogen-elevated total T₄ for hyperthyroidism.

questions.stem: This 28-day trial compares two GnRH analogs for chemical castration in advanced prostate cancer. Drug A (red) drops serum testosterone by 96% by day 3, whereas Drug B (gray) causes a 65% testosterone surge before suppressing it by day 28. Which drug classes correspond to Drug A and Drug B?
options: Drug A: dopamine D₂ agonist (cabergoline); Drug B: GH receptor antagonist (pegvisomant)
Drug A: GnRH superagonist (leuprolide); Drug B: GnRH antagonist (degarelix)
Drug A: 17α-hydroxylase inhibitor (abiraterone); Drug B: somatostatin analog (octreotide)
Drug A: GnRH antagonist (degarelix); Drug B: GnRH superagonist (leuprolide)

Drug B (gray) initially stimulates LH/FSH release (producing a 65% testosterone surge that can flare prostate cancer symptoms) before continuous receptor desensitization and down-regulation suppress testosterone to castrate levels.
choice_rationales: Cabergoline suppresses prolactin and pegvisomant blocks peripheral GH receptors; neither drives chemical castration curves.

Abiraterone blocks adrenal CYP17A1 in castration-resistant prostate cancer and octreotide inhibits GH/serotonin/VIP rather than pituitary GnRH receptors.

GnRH antagonists (-relix, such as degarelix) block GnRH receptors immediately without a flare (Drug A), whereas superagonists (leuprolide) trigger an early surge before receptor down-regulation (Drug B).

questions.tested_concept: Cabergoline D2 agonist efficacy, twice-weekly dosing, and lower dose outside BBB
questions.stem: A clinical trial of a long-acting oral ergot-derivative D₂ agonist in women with hyperprolactinemia and anovulation lowers prolactin below normal by week 4 (Panel A) and restores reproductive function in ~75% (Panel B). Why is the required dose for prolactinoma far lower than the dose used for Parkinson disease?
options: Cabergoline is metabolized into active dopamine specifically by mammary myoepithelial cells
The anterior pituitary lies outside the blood-brain barrier, permitting D₂ binding without CNS entry
Lactotropes express V₂ vasopressin receptors with 1,000-fold higher affinity than striatal D₂ receptors
Prolactinomas trap oral cabergoline via active sodium-iodide symporters
questions.explanation: Step 1. The trial shows rapid normalization of serum prolactin (<20 mcg/L by week 4) and ~75% restoration of ovulatory cycles/pregnancy with cabergoline (14-day duration, oral twice weekly). Step 2. Because the anterior pituitary sits outside the conventional blood-brain barrier, cabergoline reaches lactotrope D₂ receptors at much lower doses than needed to cross the BBB into the striatum for Parkinson disease, lowering CNS adverse effects.
choice_rationales: Cabergoline acts directly as a D₂ agonist on anterior pituitary lactotropes rather than being activated in mammary tissue.
Pituitary lactotropes sit outside the blood-brain barrier, so cabergoline suppresses prolactin and shrinks ~85% of prolactinomas at doses far below Parkinson disease therapy.
Cabergoline targets lactotrope D₂ receptors, not renal V₂ vasopressin receptors.
Sodium-iodide symporters (NIS) belong to thyroid follicular cells, not pituitary prolactinomas.

Panel B: ~75% complete restoration of ovulatory function/pregnancy with small partial-success and failure bars

questions.tested_concept: FSH follicular stimulation, hCG (LH-like) trigger shot, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
questions.stem: Transvaginal ultrasound during controlled ovarian stimulation shows multiple large dark fluid-filled ovarian follicles (dominant follicle 18.7 mm). Which agent is injected to trigger final oocyte ripening (mimicking the LH surge), and what serious complication can arise from capillary leak out of these hyperstimulated follicles?
options: Octreotide; severe dilutional hyponatremia from free-water retention
Progesterone; acute pituitary apoplexy with bitemporal hemianopia
hCG (LH mimic); ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome with ascites
Leuprolide; uterine rupture and cervical laceration during labor
questions.explanation: Step 1. Ultrasound demonstrates multiple mature fluid-filled follicles (16–18+ mm) produced by exogenous FSH stimulation. Step 2. A single injection of hCG (whose biological activity is identical to LH) serves as the trigger shot to complete oocyte maturation ~36 hours before retrieval; major risks of hyperstimulating many follicles include multiple births (~20%) and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (0.5–4%, ovarian enlargement and ascites from capillary leak).

Uterine rupture and cervical laceration are toxicities of oxytocin during labor, not hCG during IVF.

questions.tested_concept: GH direct diabetogenic vs IGF-1 anabolic effects, mecasermin, and pegvisomant
questions.stem: In this growth hormone action diagram, GH acts directly on adipose tissue (lipolysis) and liver (gluconeogenesis), while longitudinal bone growth requires hepatic Mediator X. Which drug replaces Mediator X in Laron syndrome, and which drug blocks the GH receptor in somatostatin-resistant acromegaly?
options: Cabergoline for Laron syndrome; desmopressin for acromegaly
Pegvisomant for Laron syndrome; somatropin (recombinant GH) for acromegaly
Octreotide for Laron syndrome; cosyntropin (ACTH 1–24) for acromegaly
Mecasermin (IGF-1) for Laron syndrome; pegvisomant for acromegaly
questions.explanation: Step 1. Mediator X is hepatic IGF-1 (somatomedin), which mediates GH's anabolic/somatotropic bone-growth effects (only while epiphyseal growth plates remain open), whereas GH's lipolytic and diabetogenic effects are IGF-1 independent. Step 2. Mecasermin provides recombinant IGF-1 for Laron syndrome (GH receptor defect unresponsive to GH), while pegvisomant is a pegylated GH receptor antagonist that lowers IGF-1 in acromegaly resistant to somatostatin analogs.
choice_rationales: Cabergoline inhibits prolactin (and GH/PRL co-secreting tumors), and desmopressin treats central DI.
This reverses the two drugs: pegvisomant blocks GH receptors (for acromegaly) and somatropin is recombinant GH (ineffective in Laron GH-receptor resistance).
Octreotide inhibits GH release (useful in acromegaly, not Laron syndrome), and cosyntropin tests adrenal cortisol reserve.
Mecasermin bypasses the defective GH receptor in Laron syndrome by supplying IGF-1 (Mediator X), and pegvisomant blocks peripheral GH receptors to lower IGF-1 in refractory acromegaly.

questions.stem: A 27-year-old woman treated chronically with haloperidol for schizophrenia develops secondary amenorrhea and infertility. What is the direct initial pituitary mechanism triggered by haloperidol?
options: Anterior pituitary D₂ blockade raises prolactin, which then suppresses GnRH, LH, and FSH
Direct blockade of pituitary GnRH receptors lowers LH and FSH independently of prolactin
Stimulation of hypothalamic TRH neurons lowers TSH and induces myxedema
Activation of anterior pituitary somatostatin receptors suppresses ACTH and cortisol

Decreased LH and FSH is a downstream consequence of hyperprolactinemia rather than direct GnRH receptor blockade by haloperidol.
Haloperidol blocks D₂ receptors rather than stimulating TRH or causing myxedema.
Haloperidol does not act as a somatostatin agonist or suppress ACTH.

questions.tested_concept: Vasopressin, desmopressin, oxytocin, and vaptan clinical uses and toxicities
questions.stem: A child with central diabetes insipidus is prescribed intranasal desmopressin (DDAVP) rather than native vasopressin, while a postpartum patient receives IV oxytocin for uterine atony. What shared life-threatening electrolyte toxicity can occur with vasopressin or desmopressin, and what major obstetric toxicity limits oxytocin?
options: Refractory hypernatremia from osmotic diuresis; severe osteoporosis and hot flashes
Severe hyperkalemia from aldosterone blockade; ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome
Fatal dilutional hyponatremia from free-water retention; uterine rupture or cervical laceration
Lactic acidosis from hepatic glycogenolysis; persistent hyperprolactinemia
questions.explanation: Step 1. Desmopressin selectively activates V₂ receptors (>10× antidiuretic potency of vasopressin with minimal V₁ vasoconstriction), making it ideal for central DI and enuresis, but excess free-water retention dilutes serum Na⁺ and can cause fatal hyponatremia. Step 2. Oxytocin induces uterine contractions for labor and postpartum hemorrhage, carrying a risk of uterine rupture, cervical laceration, or fetal distress if overstimulated.
choice_rationales: Vasopressin/desmopressin lower (not raise) serum Na⁺, and osteoporosis is a chronic adverse effect of GnRH analogs.
Neither drug blocks aldosterone, and ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome is a complication of gonadotropins (FSH/hCG).

Both vasopressin and desmopressin can cause fatal dilutional hyponatremia via excessive free-water retention, whereas oxytocin toxicity includes uterine rupture, cervical laceration, and neonatal trauma.
Lactic acidosis and hyperprolactinemia are not the primary toxicities of desmopressin or oxytocin.

questions.tested_concept: Peptide half-life modifications vs GH/PRL JAK2-STAT cytokine receptors
questions.stem:
Evaluate the following two statements regarding pituitary hormone pharmacology:

Statement 1: Natural short peptides (ACTH, vasopressin, oxytocin, releasing factors) signal through GPCRs with half-lives under 7 minutes; C-terminal amidation, N-terminal pyroglutamate, and synthetic D-amino acids slow peptidase degradation.
Statement 2: Growth hormone and prolactin signal through dimerized class 1 cytokine receptors coupled to cytoplasmic JAK2-STAT tyrosine kinases rather than GPCRs.
options: Both statements are true
Both statements are false
Statement 1 is true; Statement 2 is false
Statement 1 is false; Statement 2 is true
questions.explanation: Step 1. Short random-coil peptide hormones are rapidly cleaved by peptidases (<7 min half-life) and act via GPCRs; chemical modifications (amidation, pyroglutamate, D-amino acids as in DDAVP, octreotide, and leuprolide) resist proteolysis and extend duration of action. Step 2. Larger 4-helix polypeptides (GH, 191 aa; PRL, 198 aa) signal through type 1 cytokine receptor dimers activating JAK2-STAT transcription.
choice_rationales: Both statements accurately summarize peptide stability chemistry, GPCR signaling, and GH/prolactin JAK2-STAT cytokine receptor signaling.
Neither statement is false; both reflect core E6 hormone chemistry and receptor classes.
Statement 2 is also true because GH and PRL resemble class 1 cytokines (like IL-2) and signal via JAK2-STAT rather than GPCRs.
Statement 1 is also true because peptide half-lives are <7 minutes and amidation/pyroglutamate/D-amino acids resist peptidases.
